note: A key written as the escape \ud800: legal JSON grammar, not legal Unicode. Both JavaScript parsers accept it and agree byte-for-byte on the canonical form {"\ud800":1}. Python refuses -- but by accident and with the wrong error: _check_shape calls len(k.encode("utf-8")) to apply the string-length limit, an unpaired surrogate has no UTF-8 encoding, and the UnicodeEncodeError that escapes is what refuses the receipt. Nothing in the wire format excludes unpaired surrogates, and canonical_bytes handles them fine (ensure_ascii writes them straight back as \ud800), so today the answer depends on a limit check nobody aimed here. Rust refuses it too, deliberately, so the JavaScript pair are the outliers. Refusing is the right rule -- a receipt is a UTF-8 document and this one has no UTF-8 form -- but it has to be a STATED rule applied everywhere, not a side effect of measuring a length in one implementation.
